title: The Saint Michael prayer (1886)
hookLine: Leo XIII's prayer for protection, once said after every Mass

lines: ONE OF THEM: TO AN ANGEL.
cards: There was a time when a quiet Mass ended differently. The priest finished, and nobody left. He knelt at the foot of the altar, the people knelt with him, and together they prayed a few more prayers aloud.
One wasn't addressed to God the Father, or to Mary, but to an angel, and it began by asking him to defend us in battle. Some parishes have started saying it again after Mass.

teach.b: The Apocalypse says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And there was a great battle in heaven, Michael and his angels fought with the dragon." In the book of Daniel, Michael is a great prince who stands up for his people.
Scripture gives him the role of protector.

teach.h: LEO THE THIRTEENTH, AFTER LOW MASS.
teach.b: Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a short prayer to Michael in Latin and added it to the prayers said kneeling at the end of Low Mass. A story people tell says he wrote it after a frightening vision during Mass.
There's no firm record of that, and the prayer doesn't need it. When the liturgy was reformed after the Second Vatican Council, those prayers at the end of Mass were dropped.
The Saint Michael prayer itself stayed in Catholic life. Pope John Paul the Second later urged Catholics to pray it, and some parishes have brought it back. Then what it asks.
It asks Michael to defend us in battle and to be a protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. It asks God, humbly, to rebuke him.

And it asks Michael, by the power of God, to drive Satan and the evil spirits who roam the world back into hell. Strong words. But notice the order: even the warrior angel acts by God's power, not his own.
Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood."
Not against the coworker, the ex, the neighbor with the barking dog, the people on the other side of an argument. Whatever this prayer is fighting, it's never a person.

how: Some Catholics pray the Saint Michael prayer daily, and some parishes say it together at the end of Mass; it asks the archangel's protection against evil.

games.q: what does “the saint michael prayer” mean?
o: a prayer to Mary said at the end of Mass
a soldiers' prayer before going into war
a pope's prayer asking an archangel's protection

games.q: the Saint Michael prayer — tap the pairs.

s: Leo XIII's prayer to Michael was said at the end of Low Mass
it was added to the prayers said kneeling after Low Mass.
the Saint Michael prayer was banned after Vatican II
the prayers at the end of Mass were dropped; the prayer itself remained, and John Paul II urged Catholics to pray it.
the battle in the prayer is against other people
Paul: our wrestling is not against flesh and blood.

games.q: you've just prayed defend us in battle. the coworker who undermined you last week walks into the room. who's the enemy?
o: not flesh and blood: the evil at work, never the person.
nobody; the prayer is only about angels.
games.why: Paul tells the Ephesians our wrestling is not against flesh and blood. the prayer asks for protection against evil, never for victory over a person.

practice: If you know the Saint Michael prayer, or have it on a card, and you pray, say it once, slowly; if not, stay with its opening words, defend us in battle.
Bring to mind one struggle you're in right now, then do the hard part: separate the struggle from the people in it, and let anyone you've been treating as the enemy step out of the frame.
What's left is the real fight; breathe there.

wordCard.voice: The Saint Michael prayer. Pope Leo the Thirteenth's short prayer asking the archangel to defend us in battle, once said at the end of Low Mass, still prayed by some Catholics today.

orig.note: Latin: defend us in battle. Leo XIII wrote the prayer in Latin; it opens Sancte Michael Archangele, defende nos in proelio.

carryVoice: Your line: defend us in battle. Even the warrior angel acts by God's power, not his own. See you tomorrow.
